summary: Defines a MIB for information related to routing within a Fibre Channel fabric, independent of the routing protocol in use. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: This is a list of gauges that shows how traffic is routed in a storage network.

subtitle: A MIB that lets network managers view and configure the routing table of a Fibre Channel switch.

tldr.problem: Fibre Channel switches forward frames using routing tables, but there was no standard SNMP way to view or configure those routes independent of the routing protocol in use.
tldr.mechanism: The T11-FC-ROUTE-MIB module defines a per-fabric table with a last-change timestamp and a route table. Each route is matched on destination and source address masks and an optional input interface.
tldr.outcome: A manager can read or set routes for any switch and fabric, whether they came from FSPF, static configuration or another source. Write access is optional for most objects.

today: RFC 4625 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4625 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managed objects about the routing table used for routing within a Fibre Channel fabric. Objects specific to a particular routing protocol, such as the Fabric Shortest Path First (FSPF) protocol, are not in this module. FSPF has its own MIB in RFC 4626.

MIB objects are normally accessed through SNMP and defined with the Structure of Management Information, here SMIv2 (RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580). The module is independent of the routing protocol: it would still apply if a protocol other than FSPF were used.
sections.eli5: A MIB is a menu of things a network manager can ask a device about. This menu is about the directions a storage switch uses to pass messages along.

sections.title: Fibre Channel Background
sections.content:
Fibre Channel (FC) is described as a bidirectional point-to-point serial data channel. Devices called N_Ports connect through a switching network called a Fabric, or through a point-to-point link. A port on a switch that connects to an N_Port is an F_Port, and a switch port linked to another switch by an Inter-Switch Link is an E_Port.

FC frames carry 24-bit address identifiers for the source and destination ports. Fabric-assigned addresses are hierarchical: each octet is a level, and the Domain_ID is the highest. Routing within the fabric is normally done with FSPF, which lets a switch build its own table for looking up a frame's destination address to pick the outgoing link.

The newer FC-SW-4 standard adds Virtual Fabrics, where each frame is tagged to say which of several Virtual Fabrics it travels on. Frames on the same Virtual Fabric entering a Core Switch are handled by the same Virtual Switch.
sections.eli5: Think of a storage network as a town where every house has a three-part street address. Switches keep a notebook of which road to take for each address area.

sections.title: Indexes and Relationship to Other MIBs
sections.content:
This MIB goes beyond the Fibre Channel Management MIB (RFC 4044), which replaces the earlier switch-focused MIB of RFC 2837. Common textual conventions come from T11-TC-MIB in RFC 4439.

Three indexes locate a route. fcmInstanceIndex identifies a Fibre Channel management instance. fcmSwitchIndex identifies a switch within that instance. The Fabric Index distinguishes fabrics, and is always 1 when a device is attached to a single physical fabric without Virtual Fabrics. The switch index is listed before the fabric index so that one query can cover all fabrics a switch is connected to.

The module has one object group, t11FcRouteGroup, for displaying and configuring routes. It defines no managed actions invokable through SNMP.
sections.eli5: To find one line in the notebook you say which office, which switch and which town. The first two are named in other documents, and the town number is 1 unless there are several.

sections.title: The Route Table
sections.content:
The module has two tables. t11FcRouteFabricTable holds one row per management instance, switch and fabric, with a t11FcRouteFabricLastChange timestamp showing when any route row was created, modified or deleted (0 if none since restart).

t11FcRouteTable lists every route configured in or computed by a local switch for any fabric. Its index has ten objects, chosen so a manager can query by attribute without reading the whole table. All ten are integers or strings of 3 (or zero) octets, so an instance OID needs at most 22 sub-identifiers, fewer than the minimum for inetCidrRouteTable in RFC 4292.

Columns beyond the index include t11FcRouteDomainId (next-hop switch domain, which may be zero for local routes), t11FcRouteMetric (0 to 65536, meaning depends on the protocol), t11FcRouteType (local or remote, default local), t11FcRouteIfDown (remove or retain when the output interface is down, default retain), t11FcRouteStorageType and t11FcRouteRowStatus.
sections.eli5: Each row says: for messages going to this address area, send them out this door. Extra columns say how far it is and whether to keep the row if the door breaks.

sections.title: How Routes Are Matched
sections.content:
A switch takes the destination address identifier (D_ID) from a user-data frame and does a logical AND with t11FcRouteDestMask. It compares the result to t11FcRouteDestAddrId. It does the same for the source identifier (S_ID) with the source address and mask. If t11FcRouteInInterface is non-zero, the frame must also have arrived on that interface. If every check passes, the entry is a potential route.

Allowed destination masks are 255.255.255, 255.255.0 and 255.0.0. FSPF generates routes to a Domain_ID, so all FSPF routes use 255.0.0. A source address and mask of 0.0.0 match all sources.

The t11FcRouteProto value says how a route was learned. User-configured routes are netmgmt, and only those can be deleted by the user, by setting the row status to destroy.
sections.eli5: The switch covers part of the address with a stencil and checks whether what shows through matches a row. If it does, that row says which door to use.

sections.title: Compliance Requirements
sections.content:
The compliance statement makes t11FcRouteGroup mandatory. Most columns (t11FcRouteIfDown, t11FcRouteDomainId, t11FcRouteMetric, t11FcRouteType, t11FcRouteStorageType and t11FcRouteRowStatus) may be read-only, so an agent need not allow routes to be configured.

Notes inside the compliance text also say that support is not required for routes that match only a subset of source addresses, or for routes specific to particular input interfaces. Destination mask support is mandatory only for FSPF-generated routes, which means only 255.0.0 is required.
sections.eli5: The rulebook says which parts every device must show and which parts it can leave read-only. Not every device has to let you edit the notebook.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The writable objects t11FcRouteDomainId, t11FcRouteMetric, t11FcRouteType, t11FcRouteIfDown and t11FcRouteRowStatus configure new routes or change existing ones. The RFC warns that SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations, and that changing topology or network speed could let an attacker gain performance at the expense of other users.

Readable objects may also be sensitive, so even GET and NOTIFY access should be controlled, and values may need encryption in transit. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 lack adequate security, and deploying them is NOT RECOMMENDED. Implementers are RECOMMENDED to use the SNMPv3 framework with its authentication and privacy mechanisms, and operators must configure the agent so only legitimate principals can read or change these objects.
sections.eli5: Whoever can edit the direction notebook can send traffic the wrong way. Only trusted people, over a protected connection, should be allowed to change it.
